points.what: Explain what a Series (one labeled column of values) and a DataFrame (a table of Series sharing an index) are, and build small ones from lists and dictionaries.
Understand that every Series and DataFrame carries an index of row labels, and how to set, reset and use it so that labels (not just positions) identify rows.
Load a CSV file into a DataFrame with pd.read_csv and use its common options such as sep, header, index_col, usecols and dtype.
Get a quick first look at a dataset with head, tail, shape, info and describe, and read from the output the column types, non-null counts and basic statistics.
Select one column with df['col'] or several with df[['a', 'b']], and know when you get back a Series and when a DataFrame.
Select rows and columns by label with loc and by integer position with iloc, and explain how slices differ between the two.
Keep only the rows that meet one or more conditions using boolean expressions, combining them with & and | and brackets.
Create new columns and transform existing ones from other columns with vectorized arithmetic and simple column methods such as map and replace.
Recognize why chained indexing like df[df.x > 0]['y'] = 1 can fail to change the original DataFrame, what SettingWithCopyWarning means, and how to assign safely with loc or an explicit copy.
Find missing values (NaN/None) with isna and notna, and count them per column and per row to see how much of a dataset is incomplete.
Handle missing data in pandas by dropping rows or columns with dropna and by filling with fillna (a constant, the mean, or neighbouring values), and judge which choice suits a given column.
Convert columns to the right type with astype and pd.to_numeric (including errors='coerce' for messy strings) so that numeric work and models treat them correctly.
Detect duplicate rows with duplicated, remove them with drop_duplicates, and choose which columns define a duplicate and which copy to keep.
Clean text columns in bulk using the .str accessor: strip whitespace, change case, replace and extract patterns, and split strings.
Turn date and time strings into real datetime values with pd.to_datetime, handle formats and unparseable entries, and pull out parts such as year or weekday with .dt.
Inspect and tidy categorical columns with value_counts and unique, spot inconsistent labels or rare categories, and use the category dtype.
Spot unusual values using summary statistics, the IQR rule and z-scores, and decide whether an outlier is an error to fix or a real value to keep.
Order a DataFrame by one or more columns or by its index with sort_values and sort_index, in ascending or descending order.
Split data into groups with groupby, compute summaries such as mean, count or several statistics per group with agg, and read the result.
Combine two DataFrames side by side on shared keys with merge or join, and explain inner, left, right and outer joins and what happens to unmatched rows.
Stack DataFrames on top of each other (or side by side) with pd.concat, and handle mismatched columns and the resulting index.
Reshape tables between wide and long form with pivot_table and melt, and summarize one measure across two categories.
Use apply to run your own function over the rows or columns of a DataFrame, and explain why built-in vectorized operations are usually faster and clearer.
Draw line plots and scatter plots with matplotlib and add titles, axis labels, legends and colours so a plot can be read by someone else.
Explain the Figure and Axes objects, create several plots in one figure with plt.subplots, and draw on a chosen Axes.
Show how a numeric variable is distributed with histograms and compare groups or find outliers with box plots, and read both.
Make quick plots straight from a Series or DataFrame with the .plot methods (line, bar, hist, scatter, box) and pass them an Axes.
Compute a correlation matrix with df.corr, draw it as a heatmap, and interpret what correlation does and does not say, including its link to features and target.
Describe a model as a function that maps input features to a target, whose parameters are fitted from example data rather than written by hand.
Tell supervised learning (examples come with known targets) from unsupervised learning (finding structure with no target) and classify a problem as one or the other.
Decide whether a problem is regression (predict a number) or classification (predict a category) and name typical examples of each.
Explain why data is split into a training set to fit the model and a test set to estimate how it performs on new data, and why testing on the training data misleads.

Recognize overfitting (memorizing the training data) and underfitting (too simple), connect them to model complexity and the bias-variance tradeoff, and tell them apart by comparing training and test scores.
Understand data leakage, where information from the test set or the future gets into training, give common examples such as scaling before splitting, and see why it inflates scores.
